name: Wendy Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a farm assistant on the Ashby estate, which is big for round here: about two thousand acres of wheat and rapeseed and a flock of twelve hundred ewes. Callum, the farm manager, runs it for a family trust that mostly lives abroad. I'm the junior, so I do the jobs nobody else wants, mucking out the lambing shed, picking stones, chasing sheep that have got through the hedge. But I'm also the one who flies the drone over the crops and keeps the farm software up to date, because the others can't stand it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's an unusual mix for someone junior.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It is. I can tell you exactly which corner of field nine has a nitrogen problem from the drone pictures, and I still can't shear a sheep without making it look like it lost a fight. I came here two years ago after the call centre I worked at replaced most of us with an AI phone system in 2024. I use AI every day now, partly out of spite. Rob's a mechanic at the garage in town, we've got Ella, who's sixteen, and Finn, who's twelve, and our savings would cover about three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy set of tools and people oversold it. I'd still be the one saying, use it for what it's good at, like reading drone images and writing up spray records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. The call centre taught me not to fall in love with any job, so a quiet few years would let me catch my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ashby and push Callum to let me take over more of the crop planning, since the software makes it easier. I'd do my sheep handling course in the spring so I'm less useless at lambing. Same life, a bit more responsibility, hopefully a bit more pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly restless, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel safe at Ashby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than at the call centre. Callum needs me for the computer side. But the trust could sell up whenever it likes, and none of us would know until it's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would more pay mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean we stop juggling which bill to pay late. Rob's garage pays all right but not great, and Ella wants to do her driving lessons. Even an extra hundred a month changes the feel of the kitchen.

S0.say: She'd say AI is a handy set of tools that people oversold. She'd still encourage using it for what it's good at, like reading drone images and writing spray records.
S0.think: Privately she'd be both relieved and a bit disappointed by a plateau. After losing her call centre job, she'd welcome a quiet few years to catch her breath.
S0.do: Keeps working at the estate and pushes the farm manager to give her more crop planning. Takes a sheep handling course in spring and hopes for more responsibility and pay.
S0.quote: The call centre taught me not to fall in love with any job, so a quiet few years would let me catch my breath.
S0.fieldNote: She has an odd split profile: weak at hands-on stock work but the estate's tech person. Losing a call centre job to AI made her pragmatic rather than bitter. An absentee owner is a quiet background risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people like me earn our keep, so learn it now. I'd be the one at work showing the lads how to use the drone app and telling them it's not as scary as it looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Callum will buy autonomous tractors and weeding robots over a few years, and someone has to plan the jobs, check the maps and fix the glitches. I already do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Callum straight away on a trial of an autonomous sprayer, with me running it, and ask for the title and pay to match. I'd start selling drone crop scouting to the smaller farms around us on Saturdays, maybe eighty a farm. I'd get Ella using the same tools for her coursework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Excited, with a bit of nerves about the money in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would pushing for automation cost your workmates jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, and I've thought about it. Gordon's been there thirty years and he does the tractor work I'd be automating. I'd rather be the one choosing how the robot comes in than the one reading about it in the staff room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nerves about the money in between. What's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A drone that's good enough for paid scouting is a few thousand. We don't have it. I'd have to talk Callum into letting me use the estate's one, or buy a second-hand one on a loan, which makes me sweat a bit.

S1.say: She'd say steady change is when people like her earn their keep, and urge co-workers to learn now. She'd show colleagues the drone app and tell them it's less scary than it looks.
S1.think: Privately she sees steady disruption as good for her, since someone must plan and fix the autonomous machines the estate will buy. She already does that work.
S1.do: Pitches a trial autonomous sprayer that she would run, asking for a title and pay to match. Sells drone crop scouting to smaller farms on Saturdays for about eighty a farm and gets her daughter using the same tools.
S1.feel: Excited, with nerves about money in the gap before it pays.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the one choosing how the robot comes in than the one reading about it in the staff room.
S1.fieldNote: She is willing to drive automation herself and is honest about its cost to a long-serving colleague. Her main constraint is thin savings for equipment. A centrist pragmatist who prefers to shape change rather than oppose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've seen this film, the call centre went from humans to software in about eight months. I'd tell people not to wait for anyone to save them, and I'd want the government to act fast and not argue for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in trouble too, which scares me more than it scares the others. The thing that's made me useful is being good with the tech, and with full AGI the tech doesn't need me. I know exactly how fast it goes, because I've already been the person it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every penny out of the next two years: drone work every weekend, extra hours, everything into a pot. I'd cancel Ella's driving lessons for now, which she'd hate. And I'd start looking at the few jobs where people want a person, like Rob's garage front desk or the school, the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the call centre all over again, but with everyone going at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You seem more worried here than about steady change. Why such a jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because steady change needs translators, people between the machines and the old-timers. Full AGI doesn't need translators. It just talks to the tractor itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the two years matter, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means the drone business doesn't even get going before it's pointless. I'd be buying kit on a loan for a job that dies before I pay it off. So I wouldn't buy anything, I'd just hoard cash.

S2.say: She'd say she's seen this before, when her call centre moved to software in about eight months. She'd tell people not to wait to be saved and want the government to act fast.
S2.think: Privately she fears she's in trouble too, because her value is being good with technology and full AGI wouldn't need her. Having been replaced once, she knows how fast it moves.
S2.do: Saves every penny for two years from weekend drone work and extra hours, and cancels her daughter's driving lessons for now. Starts looking that week for jobs where people want a person, like the garage front desk or the school.
S2.feel: Like the call centre closure again, but with everyone losing out at once.
S2.quote: I know exactly how fast it goes, because I've already been the person it replaced.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability doesn't calm her here, because her niche as a translator between people and machines disappears. Her experience of fast automation makes her more alarmed, not less. Two years also kills the side business before it can pay off a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the time to plan, not panic. I'd post practical stuff: what skills last, what courses are free, what people did when my call centre went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me maybe three good years as the estate's tech person and some drone money. That's enough to clear the credit card and build a real cushion for the first time. Then I'd need a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a second-hand drone on a small loan in year one, and only if I had three farms signed up already. I'd put half of every drone payment into savings. By year three I'd be training for something with people in it, probably as a farm safety or animal welfare inspector, someone who has to be trusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in charge of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an inspector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people will want a human to sign off that the animals were treated right, even if robots did it. You can't shake hands with a robot when it tells you your sheep are fine. And I know the tech, so I'd know what to look for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rob say to the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say no, then he'd say show me the numbers, then he'd fix the drone's motor himself to save money. That's how we do most things. He's careful, I'm quick, and it mostly works.

S3.say: She'd say five years is a time to plan, not panic. Online she'd share practical advice on lasting skills, free courses and what happened when her call centre closed.
S3.think: Privately she expects about three good years as the estate's tech person plus some drone income. That would clear the credit card and build her first real cushion before needing a plan B.
S3.do: Buys a second-hand drone on a small loan in year one, only after signing up three farms, and saves half of each payment. By year three trains for people-trusted work like a farm safety or animal welfare inspector.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in control of it.
S3.quote: You can't shake hands with a robot when it tells you your sheep are fine.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her take a measured risk with conditions attached. She picks a future role built on human trust and sign-off. Her partnership with her careful partner is how she manages risk on thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we're smart. I'd tell people at work to pick one new skill a year and stop pretending it isn't coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a good deal for me. I'd have years of better pay running Ashby's machines, the drone business, and time to move into inspection work. Ella and Finn would be grown, and I'd be fifty-three with something to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Callum to automate in stages, with me managing it. I'd grow the drone work slowly, no big loans. Around year four I'd start the inspector training, and I'd sit Finn down about what to study, maybe something hands-on with people rather than computers, funnily enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. A little uneasy about the very end, but mostly good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: It's funny that you'd steer Finn away from computers.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, the tech nerd telling her son to avoid tech. But by the time he's working, AI will do the computer bit. I'd rather he learned to calm a frightened ewe than to write code a machine writes better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the uneasy part at the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After ten years, the inspector bit could go too, if people trust machines enough. I'd be fifty-three and I'd have to reinvent myself a third time. I could do it, I've done it twice, but I'd be tired.

S4.say: She'd call ten years plenty if people are smart. She'd urge co-workers to pick up one new skill a year and stop pretending change isn't coming.
S4.think: Privately she sees ten years as a good deal, with years of better pay, drone income and time to move into inspection work. Her children would be grown by the end.
S4.do: Pushes the estate to automate in stages under her management and grows the drone work slowly with no big loans. Starts inspector training around year four and steers her son towards hands-on people work.
S4.feel: Mostly good, with some unease about the very end.
S4.quote: I'd rather he learned to calm a frightened ewe than to write code a machine writes better.
S4.fieldNote: The tech enthusiast steers her son away from computers, which she finds funny herself. Her lingering worry is having to reinvent herself a third time at fifty-three. The decade fits her style of staged, low-debt moves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away the one thing I'm good at, which is moving quickly. What would help is cheap, fast training that's actually linked to jobs, and some money to live on while you do it. Plus a rule that firms tell workers a year ahead, not a week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people who've been automated once already. We're the early warning. Last time I learned that the people who decide these things never come and stand in the room when it happens.

headlineQuote: Last time I learned that the people who decide these things never come and stand in the room when it happens.
portrait: Wendy Fischer is a 43-year-old farm assistant on a two-thousand-acre arable and sheep estate, still clumsy with livestock but the one who flies the drone and runs the farm software. She came to farming after an AI phone system replaced most of her call centre in 2024, and now uses AI every day. She lives with her partner Rob, a mechanic, and two teenagers, with about three weeks of savings. A practical centrist, she's calm through the plateau and steady change, where she'd drive automation herself and start a drone scouting side business. Two-year AGI alarms her because it wipes out her niche, while five or ten years let her save and move towards inspection work.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because it would remove her advantage of moving quickly and her side business would die before it paid off.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast training tied to real jobs with money to live on while training, and a rule that employers warn workers a year ahead.
